## Introduction

I built this project to predict whether a tweet describes a **real
disaster** (`"Disaster"`) or **not** (`"Not Disaster"`) from its raw
text, `keyword`, and `location` fields — the classic "Real or Not? NLP
with Disaster Tweets" task. I picked it because text classification
and social-media monitoring felt like a genuinely different problem
from the tabular datasets I'd worked with before, and I wanted to see
how much of what I'd learned about imbalanced classes and model
comparison would still hold up when the features are words instead of
numbers.

Getting the data wasn't as simple as I expected. The original Kaggle
*competition* (`nlp-getting-started`) requires accepting its rules on
the website before the API will serve anything — I checked directly,
and `kaggle competitions download` returns a 403 even when I was
authenticated. I ended up using a public *dataset* mirror of the same
task instead, `vstepanenko/disaster-tweets`, which has the same 4
input columns and a larger, re-scraped sample.

Beyond just running the usual "compare class-imbalance techniques"
playbook, I wanted this project to make one point I hadn't seen spelled
out clearly elsewhere: the model that scores highest on
cross-validation isn't automatically the right one to put into
production. Below, the single best-measured model I found turned out to
be practically impossible to explain with SHAP, and choosing a
slightly-lower-scoring model instead was a deliberate tradeoff I made
on purpose, not an accident or an oversight.

## Data

```{python}
from disaster_tweets_nlp import config, data

df = data.load_tweets()
print(f"{len(df)} rows, {df.shape[1]} columns")
df[config.TARGET_COL].value_counts(normalize=True)
```

### Real data-quality issues I found by checking, not assuming

I didn't take the raw data at face value, and it's a good thing I
didn't — checking it directly turned up three real problems:

- **Exact-duplicate tweets, some with conflicting labels**: I found 147
  duplicate tweet texts, 2 of which carry *different* labels for the
  same text — genuine annotation disagreement, presumably from two
  different human labelers disagreeing. Left alone, duplicates could
  leak across a train/validation split: the model would "predict" a
  duplicate tweet in the validation set by memorizing the identical
  copy it saw during training, which inflates the validation score
  without teaching the model anything that generalizes to a genuinely
  new tweet. The 2 conflicting-label cases can't be trusted either way,
  so I dropped them rather than guess which label was right.
- **`keyword` contains raw URL-encoding artifacts**: values like
  `"mass%20murder"` instead of `"mass murder"` — the underlying scrape
  never decoded the URL-encoded parameter. This is the kind of bug that
  silently degrades a categorical feature if you don't look at the
  actual values, since `mass%20murder` and `mass murder` would be
  treated as two unrelated categories instead of one.
- **`location` is too sparse and inconsistent to use as a categorical
  feature**: 4,504 distinct free-text values across 7,952 non-null
  rows, with `"USA"`, `"United States"`, and `"US"` all counted
  separately. One-hot encoding this as-is would create thousands of
  near-useless, mostly-empty columns, so I reduced it to a simpler
  signal instead (see Feature engineering below).

```{python}
from disaster_tweets_nlp import model

X, y = data.split_features_target(df)
print(f"{len(X)} rows after cleanup (from {len(df)} raw)")
y.value_counts(normalize=True)
```

## Feature engineering

Text needed a genuinely different feature-engineering approach than
the tabular datasets I'd worked with before — I couldn't just reuse a
scaler and a one-hot encoder, since there's no "numeric column" to
scale in a tweet:

```{python}
from disaster_tweets_nlp.features import TextFeatureEngineer

engineered = TextFeatureEngineer().fit_transform(X)
engineered[["cleaned_text", "has_location", "text_length", "word_count"]].head(3)
```

- **TF-IDF** (word uni+bigrams, up to 5,000 features) on cleaned text.
  TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) turns each tweet
  into a vector of word/phrase weights: a word gets a high weight in a
  tweet if it appears often *in that tweet* but rarely across the rest
  of the dataset, which is exactly what makes a word a useful signal
  for telling tweets apart. I stripped URLs and `@mentions` first,
  since their specific characters carry no signal, and unwrapped
  hashtags to their word content so `#earthquake` contributes the word
  "earthquake" rather than a token that's technically different from
  every plain-text mention of the same word.
- **Hand-crafted numeric signals**: length, word count, and
  URL/mention/hashtag counts. These are cheap to compute — just
  counting characters and substrings — and I almost skipped them as too
  simple to matter. That assumption turned out to be wrong: as the
  interpretability section below shows, they end up mattering more than
  almost any individual word in the vocabulary.
- **`has_location`** instead of raw location text, given the cardinality
  problem above — a single yes/no flag for "was any location given at
  all" is a weaker signal than a clean location would be, but it's a
  real signal I could actually trust, unlike the raw free-text field.

## Methodology

### Why macro-F1, made concrete

```{python}
baseline = model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.logistic_estimator(), cv=5)
print(f"Accuracy: {baseline['accuracy_mean']:.4f}")
print(f"Macro-F1: {baseline['f1_macro_mean']:.4f}")
```

Accuracy (~87.8%) looked strong to me at first glance, but that's an
illusion caused by the ~81.6% majority ("Not Disaster") share — a model
that predicted "Not Disaster" for every single tweet, with zero
understanding of the text, would already score close to that number.
Macro-F1 (which averages the F1-score of each class equally, instead of
weighting by how common the class is) is noticeably lower here, and
that gap is the real story: it exposes that the Disaster class isn't
being caught nearly as well as the headline accuracy number suggests.
That's why I use macro-F1, not accuracy, for every comparison that
follows.

### Class-imbalance handling, compared honestly

Class imbalance means one class ("Not Disaster") vastly outnumbers the
other, which tends to bias a classifier toward predicting the majority
class by default, since that's the easiest way to minimize error on
average. Two common fixes are **class-weighting** (telling the model to
penalize a mistake on the minority class more heavily during training)
and **oversampling** (giving the model more copies of the minority
class to learn from). I'd have used **ADASYN** for oversampling if I
were following what I'd tried on a tabular dataset before — it
synthesizes new minority rows by finding each minority row's nearest
neighbors and interpolating between them. But that nearest-neighbor
search is a poor fit for TF-IDF's thousands of sparse, mostly-zero
dimensions: "nearest" in that space mostly picks up noise, not
meaningful similarity between tweets. So I compared class-weighting
against **`RandomOverSampler`** instead, which just duplicates existing
minority rows — a cruder but much more reliable baseline for text.

```{python}
imbalance_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"approach": "Plain Logistic Regression", **model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.logistic_estimator(), cv=5)},
    {"approach": "Logistic Regression + RandomOverSampler", **model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.logistic_estimator(), cv=5, resample=True)},
    {"approach": "Logistic Regression (class_weight=balanced)", **model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.balanced_logistic_estimator(), cv=5)},
])
imbalance_results[["approach", "f1_macro_mean", "accuracy_mean"]]
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.barh(imbalance_results["approach"], imbalance_results["f1_macro_mean"], color=[PALETTE[3], PALETTE[2], PALETTE[0]])
ax.set_xlabel("Macro-F1")
plt.show()
```

**Oversampling wins here.** This is a different result than I expected
going in — I'd assumed class-weighting would be the safer, more
reliable default, and I was a little surprised to see plain duplication
of minority rows beat it. It's not a contradiction of anything, though:
it's exactly why I measured both directly instead of assuming one
technique would generalize from one problem to the next. What helps
depends on the data and the feature space, and a high-dimensional
sparse TF-IDF space clearly behaves differently from a handful of
tabular numeric columns.

### Model comparison — and a constraint beyond macro-F1

```{python}
sweep_results = []
for name, factory in model.MODEL_FACTORIES.items():
    for resample in [False, True]:
        label = f"{name} + ROS" if resample else name
        scores = model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=factory(), cv=5, resample=resample)
        sweep_results.append({"model": label, **scores})
sweep_df = pd.DataFrame(sweep_results).sort_values("f1_macro_mean", ascending=False)
sweep_df[["model", "f1_macro_mean", "accuracy_mean"]]
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.barh(sweep_df["model"], sweep_df["f1_macro_mean"], color=PALETTE[0])
ax.set_xlabel("Macro-F1")
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.show()
```

`LightGBM + RandomOverSampler` wins here on macro-F1 — but this is
where my actual methodology diverges from "just pick the highest
number in the table," and this divergence is the single most important
decision in this project.

When I first ran this comparison, an *uncapped*-depth Random Forest
scored ~0.79 macro-F1 — higher than anything shown in the table above,
and higher than the LightGBM model I ended up shipping. My first
reaction was that I'd found my winner. But when I tried to explain that
Random Forest's predictions with SHAP (see the Model interpretability
section below), it became clear why the score looked so good: the
model had grown trees to an average depth of ~330, almost entirely by
memorizing `RandomOverSampler`'s exact-duplicate minority rows rather
than learning generalizable patterns. That depth made
`shap.TreeExplainer` take over 2 minutes to compute values for just 30
rows — completely impractical for anything I'd want to use
interactively, let alone put behind an API that needs to explain a
prediction on demand.

So I capped that Random Forest's depth to 20
(`model.random_forest_estimator`), which is a deliberate, documented
choice rather than a default. That brought it down to ~0.75 macro-F1 —
still a reasonable score, but no longer the best one. LightGBM, in
contrast, controls its tree growth with `num_leaves` (default 31)
rather than needing an explicit depth cap, so it naturally avoids the
memorization problem: it reaches the best macro-F1 in the comparison
**and** a SHAP call fast enough to use interactively (~0.5s for 300
rows). That's the model I actually trained on the full dataset and
saved for the app — chosen for being both accurate and explainable, not
for topping a leaderboard.

Why this matters beyond this one project: a model nobody can explain is
a liability the moment something goes wrong with it, however good its
raw score looks. If a "Disaster" alert gets sent out and a person
downstream asks *why* the model flagged that tweet, "I don't know, and
computing an answer takes two minutes per prediction" is not a usable
answer for a real system — whereas a fast, reliable SHAP explanation is
something a human reviewer can actually check in real time. Picking the
highest cross-validation number without checking whether the model is
explainable is, in effect, optimizing for a number nobody downstream
can act on.

## Choosing a decision threshold

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, classification_report

disaster_proba = model.cross_val_disaster_probabilities(X, y, cv=5)
disaster_preds_default = (disaster_proba >= 0.5).astype(int)
y_numeric = (y == "Disaster").astype(int)
print(classification_report(y_numeric, disaster_preds_default, target_names=["Not Disaster", "Disaster"], digits=3))
```

A classifier like this doesn't just output "Disaster" or "Not
Disaster" — it outputs a probability, and a **decision threshold** is
the cutoff probability above which I call a tweet "Disaster." The
default of 0.5 is just a convention, not something the model itself
requires; nothing stops me from lowering it to catch more real
disasters at the cost of more false alarms, or raising it to be more
conservative. At the default threshold, Disaster recall is ~75% (I
catch about three-quarters of real disaster tweets) and precision is
~55% (a bit better than a coin flip on which flagged tweets are real) —
a genuinely usable detector, though far from perfect. Since the
threshold is a free choice rather than something fixed by the model,
the next step sweeps it directly to see what the tradeoff actually
looks like at other cutoffs.

```{python}
pr_auc = average_precision_score(y_numeric, disaster_proba)
print(f"Average precision (PR-AUC): {pr_auc:.4f}  (base rate: {y_numeric.mean():.4f})")

threshold_sweep = model.threshold_sweep(y, disaster_proba, target_recalls=[0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9])
threshold_sweep
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(threshold_sweep["recall"], threshold_sweep["precision"], marker="o", color=PALETTE[0])
for _, row in threshold_sweep.iterrows():
    ax.annotate(f"thr={row['threshold']:.2f}", (row["recall"], row["precision"]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(6, 4))
ax.axhline(y_numeric.mean(), linestyle="--", color="gray", label="base rate")
ax.set_xlabel("Recall (share of real disaster tweets caught)")
ax.set_ylabel("Precision (share of \"Disaster\" alerts that are real)")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

PR-AUC (average precision, computed by averaging precision across every
possible threshold) summarizes the whole precision/recall tradeoff in
one number, rather than reporting just one cutoff. The PR-AUC here
(~0.71) is roughly **3.9x the base rate** (~0.18) — which is my
shorthand for "how much better than blind guessing is this curve,
overall." That's a stronger lift than I expected walking in. Even at 90%
recall (catching 9 out of 10 real disaster tweets), precision stays
above 38%, which tells me the tweet text itself genuinely carries a lot
of usable signal for this task, more than I'd have guessed before
looking at the numbers.

## Model interpretability

I used **SHAP** (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to understand what the
final LightGBM model is actually paying attention to, rather than
trusting it as a black box just because its score was good. SHAP
assigns each feature a contribution value for each individual
prediction — how much that specific feature pushed the prediction
toward "Disaster" or away from it — based on game-theory ideas about
fairly splitting credit among contributors. For a tree-based model like
LightGBM, `shap.TreeExplainer` computes these values by walking the
model's actual trees, which is what makes it fast enough to run
interactively here (as opposed to a model-agnostic explainer, which
would need to re-run the model many times per prediction and would have
been far too slow for the same reason the uncapped Random Forest was
impractical above). Averaging the absolute SHAP value of each feature
across many tweets gives a ranking of which features matter most
overall, which is what the chart below shows.

```{python}
from disaster_tweets_nlp.interpretability import compute_shap_values, top_shap_features

final_pipeline = model.train_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.lightgbm_estimator(), resample=True)
explanation, _ = compute_shap_values(final_pipeline, X, max_samples=300)
top = top_shap_features(explanation, top_n=15).sort_values("mean_abs_shap")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
ax.barh(top["feature"], top["mean_abs_shap"], color=PALETTE[0])
ax.set_xlabel("Mean |SHAP value|")
ax.set_title("Top 15 features")
plt.show()
```

`text_length` and `word_count` dominate every other feature by a wide
margin, which genuinely surprised me — I expected specific
disaster-related words to lead the ranking, not two simple counts I'd
almost skipped adding. My best explanation: real disaster tweets (often
news-style reports) tend to be longer and more detail-dense than casual
tweets that merely use disaster-adjacent words figuratively (e.g. "this
traffic is a disaster"). Beyond those two, specific words do carry real
signal too (`killed`, `collision`, `warning`, place names), but they
matter much less than the two structural, hand-crafted numeric
features. This is a finding I wouldn't have without deliberately
engineering those simple counts alongside the TF-IDF vocabulary — if
I'd relied on TF-IDF word features alone, I'd have missed the single
strongest signal in the whole model.

## Discussion: what this project doesn't do

I classified individual tweets as disaster-related or not — I want to
be upfront that this is a genuinely narrower problem than a real
disaster-response or emergency-triage system would need to solve:

- **No real-time stream processing.** My model scores tweets one at a
  time, in batch. An actual monitoring system needs to ingest a live
  stream, deduplicate near-identical retweets/reposts (a much harder
  version of the exact-duplicate check I did here), and rate-limit
  alerts so a viral non-disaster tweet doesn't flood a response team.
- **No geolocation.** `has_location` is the only signal I kept from the
  `location` field, specifically because the raw text was too
  inconsistent to parse reliably. A real system would need proper
  geocoding — resolving free-text location mentions to actual
  coordinates — which is a substantial NLP problem of its own, not
  something I attempted here.
- **No verification or severity ranking.** My model answers "is this
  about a disaster," not "is this true" or "how severe is it." Both are
  necessary next questions before anyone could act on an alert from
  this model.
- **No temporal/event clustering.** Real disaster response cares about
  detecting an *emerging event* — a spike in related tweets about the
  same incident — not just classifying tweets independently. That's a
  clustering/trend-detection problem layered on top of the per-tweet
  classification I built, and it's not something my current
  architecture does at all.

None of this is a limitation specific to how I executed this project —
it's the honest scope boundary between "classify this tweet's topic"
and "build a disaster-response monitoring system," and I'd rather state
that boundary plainly than let the model's decent numbers imply
something bigger than what it actually does.

## Conclusion

Working through a moderately imbalanced, real text-classification
dataset gave me a few honest, measured findings I hadn't fully
appreciated before starting: accuracy overstates performance here, just
as I'd expect on any imbalanced dataset, even though the imbalance
itself is moderate rather than extreme; oversampling beat
class-weighting for TF-IDF features, which was a different result than
I expected going in; and the strongest-scoring model I measured wasn't
the one I shipped, because scoring highest on macro-F1 and being
practical to explain with SHAP turned out to be in direct tension with
each other. Choosing the production model on that basis — not on the
single highest number in a sweep — is the main methodological point I
wanted this project to make, and I think it generalizes well beyond
this one dataset: a model's raw score is only half the story if nobody
can explain why it made a given prediction. Real disaster-response
triage remains a substantially larger problem than what I built here,
and I'd rather state that scope boundary plainly than blur it.
